taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Kew treats Eragrostis intermedia var. appressa and Eragrostis lugens var. major as synonyms of the species; learner remains species-level.
look_here_first: PLAINS LOVEGRASS: real source-labelled photographs show a fine, OPEN delicate panicle of tiny dark spikelets and a true basal tussock in dry rocky ground. Typical mature sheath BODY is relatively smooth, with hairs more concentrated at throat/collar; lower panicle axils can ALSO bear hairs, so one tuft is not decisive. Compare bigtop hirsute sheaths and taller sand lovegrass; confirm collar and measured ripe spikelets for difficult specimens.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts E. intermedia and lists Texas in its native range. Hagenbuch & Lemke's Texas Hill Country grass treatment cites multiple Hays County specimens (Breckenridge 457, Jessup 57, Lemke 674, Lyday 281, Ruiseco 11). The same treatment cites Gillespie County specimen Sanchez 960. The same treatment cites Val Verde County specimens Labus 129 and 197; it also cites a Bandera/Medina County collection.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: County PASS is based on cited herbarium vouchers in a regional grass treatment, not broad ecoregion presence or seeded roadside/landscape occurrences.

best_field_traits: perennial, caespitose/tufted grass with erect culms commonly around 30–75 cm
leaves basal and cauline; blades narrow, roughly 1–5 mm wide
leaf sheaths mostly glabrous to only sparsely papillose, with hairs near the apex/collar
ligule a very short fringe/line of hairs
panicle very open and broadly ovoid, often occupying a large fraction of plant height
panicle branch axils only sparsely hairy, especially at lower nodes
primary panicle branches bare for a distance near their bases
pedicels mostly much longer than the small spikelets and divergent
spikelets small, green to purple-tinged, generally with only a few florets
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Eragrostis hirsuta: Bigtop lovegrass is conspicuously hairier: its leaf sheaths are hirsute and panicle branch axils are bearded. It is commonly taller with a larger panicle. E. intermedia has mostly smooth sheaths and only sparse axillary hairs. Eragrostis trichodes: Sand lovegrass often shows conspicuous long hair tufts at the sheath apex/collar and a taller, narrow-based plant with a large diffuse panicle; use sheath/collar hair placement and spikelet/panicle architecture rather than overall airiness alone. Eragrostis cilianensis: Stinkgrass is an annual with a much coarser, denser-looking panicle and gland-dotted lemmas; crushed young plants may have a strong odor. It is introduced in Texas.
crew_field_walkthrough: PLAINS LOVEGRASS: real source-labelled photographs show a fine, OPEN delicate panicle of tiny dark spikelets and a true basal tussock in dry rocky ground. Typical mature sheath BODY is relatively smooth, with hairs more concentrated at throat/collar; lower panicle axils can ALSO bear hairs, so one tuft is not decisive. Compare bigtop hirsute sheaths and taller sand lovegrass; confirm collar and measured ripe spikelets for difficult specimens.
On the SAME mature plant, compare full sheath-body hair distribution versus throat, then actual lower branch-axil and mature spikelet with scale.
If photo lacks collar and true spikelet characters, teach genus-level ID and mark the remaining photo tasks.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Same-plant sheath surface + actual collar with 10× macro
Several lower branch axils in focus
Mature attached spikelets with glumes and ruler, reconcile source disagreement on pedicel length
field_identification_cautions: Purple hue and general airy-panicle appearance overlap among several local lovegrasses.

Some published descriptions disagree on pedicel-to-spikelet length and typical floret number. Do not build a yes/no key from either alone until source concepts and locally vouchered specimens are reconciled.
Hairs at the panicle branch axils are not unique to E. hirsuta; distinguish diffuse sheath hairiness from a few localized tufts.
Do not infer a finished diagnostic photo, a measured structure or an accurate arrow from an image filename or role caption. Validate the actual pixels.
morphology_keys.what_to_teach_crew: PLAINS = open fine panicle plus mostly smooth sheath (hair concentrated at opening). Look for an airy head, then verify WHERE the hairs grow. Never distinguish plains vs sand from the cloud alone.

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. hirsuta usually has more conspicuous hairs on the sheath surface/margins and bearded panicle axils; E. trichodes commonly has a taller, elongated diffuse panicle and long hairs concentrated at the sheath throat, with spikelets sometimes near branch tips. E. spectabilis can make an exceptionally broad loose purple tumbleweed-like panicle. Witchgrass (Panicum capillare) has a different spikelet construction; dissect before using color or openness.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Plains lovegrass: a cloud is a CLUE, not a conclusion
steps: Photograph an intact open mature head and its small, distinct spikelets (the existing photo arrows teach this only).
Move DOWN the same stem: photograph sheath surface plus apex/margins, collar and hair-fringe ligule, sharp enough to show hair distribution.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — OPEN PANICLE + SHEATH
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fine, widely spreading perennial panicle; inspect mostly smooth sheath BODY before deciding.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Start with the existing source-labelled in-ground habit photograph (panel 3), the genuine collected fibrous-rooted crown (panel 5), and an open pyramidal flowering head (USFS reports culms about 30–90 cm, panicles about 15–35 cm). Follow the same stem down to its sheath: plains lovegrass is often relatively smooth on the sheath body, with hairs concentrated near the throat; occasional sheath hairs and bearded lower branch axils occur, so 'hairless' is not an absolute rule. Purple hue or a cloudlike head alone is not a species diagnosis.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ROOTED CROWN AND HABIT PHOTOS AVAILABLE — SAME-PLANT TEXAS FLOWERING VOUCHER NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · FIND THE TRUE LIGULE, NOT OUTER HAIRS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Inner ligule only about 0.2–0.4 mm; outer collar/throat hairs may be much longer.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open a mature blade at its INNER blade–sheath junction and photograph at 10–20× with a 1-mm scale. Go Botany describes a 0.2–0.4 mm hair-fringed or membranous-ciliate ligule. The conspicuous hairs behind the throat are separate; do not draw a ligule arrow on a distant sheath photograph. Compare hair distribution on at least two sheaths from the same plant. Bob Harms' existing panel 4 shows the authentic collar/sheath region and a source scale, but does NOT independently isolate the free inner 0.2–0.4 mm ligule.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SCALED EXTERIOR COLLAR AVAILABLE — TRUE INNER LIGULE STILL NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · TRACE PANICLE BRANCHES AND PEDICELS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Open 15–35 cm panicle; tiny spikelets on delicate divergent stalks.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Find a complete mature panicle and photograph the lower branch junctions and several attached spikelet pedicels. USFS describes a diffuse pyramidal panicle; published pedicel-to-spikelet length and floret counts conflict between Texas A&M and UT/FNA-related treatments. Do NOT use a single rigid pedicel-ratio cutoff, and do not treat a few axillary hairs as proof of bigtop lovegrass.
field_id_short_tiles.status: OPEN PANICLE PHOTOS AVAILABLE — LOWER AXIL AND PEDICEL SCALE NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE A MATURE MULTIFLORETED SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: Spikelets about 3–7 mm in Go Botany; broader 3–10 mm reported in a Texas treatment.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Isolate two or three fully mature, laterally compressed spikelets with a physical millimeter rule; Go Botany reports 3–7 mm and more than one floret, while the historical Texas treatment reports 2–9 florets and 3–10 mm. Count individual overlapping florets, not panicle branches. Treat published variation as a source-concept comparison, not an unverified measurement of archived photographs. Bob Harms' existing panel 6 already shows source-identified mature spikelets with a millimeter scale; do not request another generic spikelet view. Remaining work is to verify floret counts and any conflicting measurement ranges on attached material.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SCALED MATURE SPIKELETS AVAILABLE — FLORET COUNT / SOURCE CONCEPT QA

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · SEPARATE BOTH GLUMES AND AN AWNLESS LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume ~1–1.2 mm, upper ~1.3–2 mm; lemma ~1.8–2.2 mm, 3-veined and AWNLESS.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Published Go Botany gives upper glume 1.3–2 mm, lemma 1.8–2.2 mm and a 0-mm lemma awn; a historical Texas description reports lower glume ~1–1.2 mm and lemma ~1.8–2.5 mm. At 20–40× dissect the basal pair of one-veined glumes and a mature three-veined fertile lemma/palea. Do not confuse the upper glume with the first lemma or fabricate glume-nerve arrows on a whole-head photograph. Bob Harms' panel 7 already shows a real separated lemma, palea and grain with source scale. Do not call all dissection anatomy missing: specifically resolve lower/upper glume attachment and individual vein counts at suitable magnification.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL SCALED LEMMA/PALEA DISSECTION AVAILABLE — GLUME/VEIN MACRO GAP

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES + PUBLIC GATE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Plains vs bigtop vs sand: inspect WHERE sheath hairs grow, then measure spikelets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: E. hirsuta often has conspicuous hairs across the sheath BODY and bearded panicle axils; E. trichodes is usually taller with longer hairs concentrated at the sheath THROAT and a large oblong head. E. spectabilis makes a broad, often tumbling flowering cloud. Color, a single hairy axil and a single airy photograph are not decisive. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same authenticated Central Texas plant linking the rooted crown to a mature head; opened and measured inner ligule; lower branch axils; separate glume bases and lemma veins if not resolved by existing scaled Bob Harms panels. Existing panels 5–7 already document real roots, scaled spikelets and separated lemma/palea. NEEDS_SITE_QA: review ten current panels, ten image records, ten existing markers, original licenses including CC BY-NC exclusions where applicable, identity/attribution, all arrow endpoints, and public mobile rendering. Remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
